text: Every IAM policy you've written so far probably works. The harder question is whether it grants exactly what you meant it to, or something quietly broader. In this lesson we're pulling apart the policy document itself — Effect, Action, Resource, Condition — and the evaluation logic behind it, so a policy that passes testing doesn't also pass a credential leak straight into a bigger blast radius than you intended.

Every policy, identity-based or resource-based, is built from the same fields. Effect is Allow or Deny, nothing else. Action lists the API operations in service colon operation syntax. Resource lists the exact ARNs the statement covers — and this is the field most policies get wrong by being too loose. Condition narrows things further: it only applies when a stated circumstance is actually true.

Action star on S3 grants every S3 operation that exists today, including PutBucketPolicy, plus everything AWS adds later, automatically. Resource star does the same thing to scope instead of verb — a tightly scoped Action combined with a wildcard Resource still reaches every bucket in the account, including ones created after the policy was written. Scoping Resource to a specific ARN, or an ARN prefix with the wildcard only on the object key, keeps a leaked credential's reach limited to what it was actually supposed to touch.

Condition answers under what circumstances, not what or where. aws:SourceIp restricts a grant to a known network range. aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent requires the session to have authenticated with MFA before a destructive action like deleting a bucket is allowed. aws:RequestedRegion stops a grant from being usable somewhere your workload has no business running. None of these ever widen the Action or Resource grant — they only ever narrow it.

A single principal can have several policies in play at once, and IAM's evaluation order is fixed. First, an explicit Deny anywhere wins, full stop, no matter how many Allow statements also match. Second, an explicit Allow is required — there is no implicit allow in IAM. Third, everything else defaults to deny. That ordering is exactly why one overly broad Allow statement is dangerous, and one well-placed Deny is powerful.

Scoped IAM policies cap what a single principal can do. Next lesson moves up a level: AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies, which cap what any IAM policy in an entire account — or an entire organizational unit — is even allowed to grant in the first place.
